query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron (≈0.1 at.%) during synthesis of refractory high‐entropy alloys will induce the formation of finely dispersed intergranular boride precipitates that promote a serrated grain boundary morphology, thereby enhancing grain boundary cohesion and reducing local strain concentrations under high-temperature loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr) produced by methods such as mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, displaying a predominantly BCC solid‐solution structure with straight (planar) grain boundaries and only moderate elevated-temperature ductility and creep resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled trace addition of boron (approximately 0.1 at.%) into the alloy during processing.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing conditions (e.g., tensile and creep tests at around 650°C and above) typical of extreme environments such as next-generation nuclear reactors or aerospace applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale intergranular boride precipitates that catalyze the development of a serrated grain boundary morphology.
generation.mechanism: Boron reacts during processing to form fine boride precipitates at grain and phase boundaries. These precipitates impede grain boundary migration and promote boundary undulation (serration) during subsequent heat treatments. The serrated boundaries are less prone to localized strain concentration and intergranular cracking during creep or tensile deformation at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing overall mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy with boron-induced serrated grain boundaries is expected to exhibit higher elevated-temperature ductility, increased creep rupture life, and reduced minimum creep strain rates relative to a baseline alloy with straight grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy processed without boron addition, which typically shows straight grain boundaries and lower high-temperature tensile ductility and creep resistance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to work in refractory high-entropy alloys possessing a BCC-dominated matrix where minor boron additions can stably form intergranular borides. It may not be effective in alloy systems that do not favor boride formation or in those where excessive precipitate coarsening occurs at very high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on combining evidence from studies showing that minor boron additions improve grain boundary cohesion (e.g., PMC9572892) with results where serrated grain boundaries markedly enhanced high-temperature mechanical properties in HEAs (e.g., PMC9848264). However, the specific relationship between trace boron-induced precipitates and the development of serrated boundaries in refractory HEAs has not yet been explored, leaving uncertainties regarding the kinetics of boride formation and its thermal stability in extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory HEA samples using identical processing conditions (mechanical alloying and SPS), with one set doped with 0.1 at.% boron and one set without boron. After identical homogenization and heat-treatment steps, perform elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests at around 650°C. Use electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to characterize the grain boundary morphology and verify the presence or absence of boride precipitates.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain at 650°C
Minimum creep strain rate and creep rupture life under a constant load at 650°C
Microstructural analysis of grain boundaries for serration and boride precipitate distribution using SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., in tensile ductility and creep life) compared to the undoped baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to show a transition from straight to serrated grain boundaries due to boride precipitation, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
